title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt XXXV: The Last Boast (lines 2460–2601)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 92–98, lines 2460–2601 (fitt XXXV). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Gewīteð þonne on sealman, sorhlēoð gæleð
ān æfter ānum;
sentences.l: Goes then to his bed, sings a sorrow-song, one after one;
sentences.i: Then he goes to his bed and sings a song of sorrow, the one man for the one he has lost;
sentences.n: The subject, ‘he’, is not named: it is the grieving father of the comparison that ended the last part (the old man whose son hangs on the gallows, 2444–2459), and the sentence carries on from there. ‘Gewīteð’ is ‘goes’ (present of ‘gewītan’), ‘on sealman’ is ‘to his bed’ (‘sealma’, ‘couch’), and ‘sorhlēoð gæleð’ is ‘sings a sorrow-song’ (‘sorh’ ‘sorrow’ + ‘lēoð’ ‘song’; ‘galan’ ‘sing, chant’). ‘ān æfter ānum’ is literally ‘one after one’; I take it as ‘the one for the other’, the living man for the dead, which is a reading and not a certainty.

sentences.t:
þūhte him eall tō rūm,
wongas ond wīcstede.
sentences.l: it seemed to him all too roomy, the plains and the dwelling-places.
sentences.i: everything seemed far too wide for him, the fields and the homesteads.
sentences.n: ‘þūhte’ is ‘seemed’ (preterite of ‘þyncan’), the impersonal verb taking ‘him’ in the dative, and ‘tō rūm’ is ‘too roomy’: empty space is the measure of loss. ‘wongas’ (‘plains, fields’) and ‘wīcstede’ (‘dwelling-places’, ‘wīc’ ‘dwelling’ + ‘stede’ ‘place’) are the two things that seemed too big, one standing for the land and one for the house.

sentences.t:
Swā Wedra helm
æfter Herebealde heortan sorge
weallinde wæg; wihte ne meahte
on ðām feorhbonan fǣghðe gebētan;
sentences.l: So the helm of the Weders bore welling heart-sorrow for Herebeald; in no way could he on the life-slayer make good the feud;
sentences.i: So the protector of the Weders carried, welling up in his heart, sorrow for Herebeald; in no way could he make the feud good against the one who had taken his son’s life;
sentences.n: ‘Swā’ ties the comparison to the story it stands for. ‘Wedra helm’ is ‘helm (protector) of the Weders’, a title for Hrethel, king of the Geats (‘Wedras’ is another name for the Geats); ‘helm’ is the head-covering that guards the head, hence ‘protector’. ‘wæg’ is the preterite of ‘wegan’, ‘bore’, and ‘weallinde’ (‘welling, boiling’) agrees with ‘sorge’. ‘feorhbonan’ is ‘life-slayer’, the dative of the man who killed: Hæthcyn, Hrethel’s own son, who shot his elder brother Herebeald dead by accident (told in 2435–2443). ‘fǣghðe gebētan’ is ‘make good the feud’: a killing is normally paid for in blood or wergild, and here the killer is the king’s other son, so no payment can be exacted.

sentences.t:
nō ðȳ ǣr hē þone heaðorinc hatian ne meahte
lāðum dǣdum, þēah him lēof ne wæs.
sentences.l: none the sooner could he hate the warrior with hostile deeds, though he was not dear to him.
sentences.i: yet he could no more hate the warrior for it with hostile deeds, though that man was no favourite of his.
sentences.n: ‘nō ðȳ ǣr’ is ‘none the sooner’, ‘ðȳ’ being the instrumental of ‘þæt’ (‘by that’) and ‘ǣr’ ‘earlier’. ‘lāðum dǣdum’ is a dative of means, ‘with hostile deeds’ (‘lāð’ ‘hateful, hostile’): he could not turn his grief into hatred and action. ‘þēah him lēof ne wæs’ is ‘though he was not dear to him’; the sentence admits that Hæthcyn was not specially loved, and still the father could not strike at him. ‘him’ is the father (dative) and ‘lēof’ is nominative, agreeing with the warrior who killed the son.

sentences.t:
Hē ðā mid þǣre sorhge, þē him tō sār belamp,
gumdrēam ofgeaf, Godes lēoht gecēas;
sentences.l: He then with that sorrow, which had befallen him too sorely, gave up men’s joy, chose God’s light;
sentences.i: Then, with the grief that had come on him too sorely to bear, he gave up the joy of men and chose God’s light;
sentences.n: ‘Hē’ is Hrethel; ‘mid þǣre sorhge’ is ‘with that sorrow’, and ‘þē him tō sār belamp’ a relative clause, ‘which befell him too sorely’ (‘belimpan’, ‘befall’). Klaeber’s italic ‘t’ in ‘tō’ marks an alteration. The apparatus records that the manuscript has ‘sio’ in this half-line, which editors read as ‘swā’ (‘so’) or ‘giō’ (‘formerly’) or drop, but it does not say exactly what lies behind Klaeber’s ‘tō’, so this half-line is shaky. ‘gumdrēam ofgeaf’ is ‘gave up men’s joy’ (‘gum’ ‘man’ + ‘drēam’ ‘joy, revelry’): he left the hall and its company. ‘Godes lēoht gecēas’, ‘chose God’s light’, is the poet’s way of saying he died and went to heaven.

sentences.t:
eaferum lǣfde, swā dēð ēadig mon,
lond ond lēodbyrig, þā hē of līfe gewāt.
sentences.l: to his heirs he left, as a blessed man does, land and people-fortress, when he departed from life.
sentences.i: As a fortunate man does, he left to his heirs his land and his people’s stronghold when he departed this life.
sentences.n: ‘eaferum’ is a dative plural, ‘to his heirs’ (Hæthcyn and Hygelac, the sons left to him), and ‘lǣfde’ ‘left’; the object ‘lond ond lēodbyrig’ comes last. ‘swā dēð ēadig mon’ is ‘as a blessed man does’ (‘ēadig’ ‘prosperous, fortunate’): a man in good standing hands on his holdings to his sons, even when he dies of grief. ‘lēodbyrig’ is ‘people-fortress’ (‘lēod’ ‘people’ + ‘byrig’, the accusative singular of ‘burg’), the fortified seat of the nation.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs synn ond sacu Swēona ond Gēata
ofer wīd wæter wrōht gemǣne,
herenīð hearda, syððan Hrēðel swealt,
sentences.l: Then was crime and strife of Swedes and Geats, over the wide water a quarrel in common, hard war-malice, after Hrethel died,
sentences.i: Then there was enmity and strife between Swedes and Geats, a quarrel shared across the wide water, a bitter war-hatred, after Hrethel died,
sentences.n: ‘synn ond sacu’ is ‘hostility and strife’, a pair of near-synonyms (‘synn’ is ‘sin, crime, wrong’ and here ‘enmity’); ‘wrōht gemǣne’ is ‘a quarrel in common’, shared by both sides. The two peoples stand in the genitive (‘Swēona ond Gēata’), ‘of the Swedes and the Geats’. ‘herenīð’ is ‘war-malice’ (‘here’ ‘army’ + ‘nīð’ ‘hostility’). Klaeber’s italic ‘w’ in ‘wīd’ marks an alteration; the apparatus gives the reading of the manuscript (as copied in the transcript marked A) as ‘rid’, and ‘wīd’ is Grundtvig’s repair, so ‘wide’ is an editor’s guess at a half-lost word. The poem does not name the ‘wide water’ that lay between the two peoples. ‘syððan Hrēðel swealt’ is ‘after Hrethel died’ (‘sweltan’ ‘die’), the point from which the strife is counted.

sentences.t:
oððe him Ongenðeowes eaferan wǣran
frome fyrdhwate, frēode ne woldon
ofer heafo healdan, ac ymb Hrēosnabeorh
eatolne inwitscear oft gefremedon.
sentences.l: or Ongentheow’s sons were bold, army-keen: they would not keep peace over the seas, but around Hreosnabeorh often wrought terrible malice-slaughter.
sentences.i: or rather, Ongentheow’s sons were bold and eager for the campaign, and would not keep the peace across the sea, but around Hreosnabeorh often did dreadful treacherous slaughter.
sentences.n: ‘oððe’ is ‘or’; it offers a second way of saying what kept the strife going, and in the idiomatic line I give it as ‘or rather’. ‘him’ (‘to them’) is a loose dative, and I do not try to render it. ‘frome fyrdhwate’ are two adjectives with ‘eaferan’: ‘bold’ and ‘army-keen’ (‘fyrd’ ‘army’ + ‘hwæt’ ‘keen’). ‘frēode’ is ‘peace, friendship’ (accusative), ‘healdan’ ‘keep’, ‘ofer heafo’ ‘over the seas’ (the apparatus records Sarrazin’s ‘heaþo’, which would be ‘over battle’). ‘Hrēosnabeorh’ is ‘Hreosnabeorh’, a hill, evidently in Geatland since the Swedes raid there (the apparatus lists the reading ‘Hrefna beorh’, ‘Raven’s hill’, of Bugge and Sedgefield). ‘inwitscear’ is ‘malice-slaughter’ (‘inwit’ ‘malice, treachery’ + ‘scear’, from ‘sceran’ ‘cut’, so literally ‘malice-cutting’); the exact sense of ‘scear’ is a guess from the root. Ongentheow is the Swedish king; the next lines allude to Hæthcyn’s death in this strife.

sentences.t:
Þæt mǣgwine mīne gewrǣcan,
fǣhðe ond fyrene, swā hyt gefrǣge wæs,
sentences.l: That my kinsmen-friends avenged, the feud and the crime, as it was known by report,
sentences.i: That feud and that crime my kinsmen avenged, as is well known,
sentences.n: ‘Þæt’ is the object of ‘gewrǣcan’ (‘avenged’), put first for emphasis and picked up by ‘fǣhðe ond fyrene’ (‘the feud and the crime’), the thing avenged. Beowulf is speaking, so ‘mǣgwine mīne’ are ‘my kinsmen-friends’ (‘mǣg’ ‘kinsman’ + ‘wine’ ‘friend’): the Geat princes, as his own kin through Hygelac. ‘swā hyt gefrǣge wæs’ is ‘as it was known by hearsay’, a stock phrase for what everyone had heard.

sentences.t:
þēah ðe ōðer his ealdre gebohte,
heardan cēape;
sentences.l: though one of them bought with his life, at a hard bargain;
sentences.i: though one of them paid for it with his life, a hard bargain;
sentences.n: ‘þēah ðe’ is ‘though’, ‘ōðer’ ‘the one, one of the two’ (one of the kinsmen just spoken of), and ‘ealdre’ is a dative of price, ‘with his life’ (‘ealdor’ ‘life’); ‘gebohte’ is ‘bought’, with no object in Klaeber’s text, and ‘heardan cēape’ ‘at a hard bargain’ (‘cēap’ ‘purchase, price’) is a dative of price too. The one who paid is Hæthcyn, named next. The apparatus shows that editors disagree about how to fill out the half-line: Klaeber’s ‘his’ is shared by Holder, Holthausen and Chambers, while others read ‘hit’ (‘it’) or insert it: the grammar is not fully certain, though the sense of paying with one’s life is clear.

sentences.t:
Hæðcynne wearð,
Gēata dryhtne gūð onsǣge.
sentences.l: to Hæthcyn, lord of the Geats, war became fatal.
sentences.i: For Hæthcyn, lord of the Geats, the war ended in death.
sentences.n: ‘Hæðcynne’ and ‘Gēata dryhtne’ are datives, ‘to Hæthcyn, to the lord of the Geats’, and ‘wearð’ ‘became’. ‘onsǣge’ is a hard word, adjective or noun, ‘falling upon, attack’; I take ‘fatal’ as a guess from the context. Hæthcyn was Hrethel’s second son and so the brother of Beowulf’s mother, Beowulf’s uncle.

sentences.l: Then I heard in the morning that one kinsman avenged the other with the edges of a blade on the slayer, where Ongentheow seeks out Eofor;
sentences.i: Then, in the morning, I have heard, one kinsman avenged the other on his slayer with the edges of the blade, where Ongentheow went for Eofor;
sentences.n: ‘gefrægn’ is ‘heard, learned by asking’ (the usual word for what the poet knows by report), and it governs the accusative and infinitive ‘mǣg ōðerne … on bonan stǣlan’, ‘that one kinsman … [avenged] on the slayer’. ‘stǣlan’ I take as ‘avenge’ (the lexica give ‘put to the charge of, avenge’), which is a reading I accept from them, not a certainty. Who the ‘kinsman’ is, and who ‘the other’, is not spelled out in this clause. I take the slayer to be Ongentheow, who killed Hæthcyn, and the blow to be Eofor’s (a warrior of Hygelac’s following), because the next lines show Eofor striking Ongentheow down; that identification is inferred from the story, not stated here. ‘nīosað’ takes the genitive ‘Eofores’, and means ‘seeks out, attacks’; it is a present tense where the story is past, a historic present (Grein reads the past ‘nīosade’). So Ongentheow went for Eofor and was cut down.

sentences.t:
gūðhelm tōglād, gomela Scylfing
hrēas [hilde]blāc; hond gemunde
fǣhðo genōge, feorhsweng ne oftēah.
sentences.l: The war-helm slid apart, the old Scylfing fell battle-pale; the hand remembered feuds enough, did not hold back the life-stroke.
sentences.i: The war-helm burst asunder, and the old Scylfing fell pale in battle; the hand remembered its many feuds and held back nothing of the death-blow.
sentences.n: ‘gūðhelm’ is ‘war-helm’, ‘tōglād’ the preterite of ‘tōglīdan’, ‘slide apart, burst open’. ‘gomela Scylfing’ is ‘the old Scylfing’, Ongentheow (the Scylfings are the Swedish royal house). ‘hrēas’ is ‘fell’. The bracket in ‘[hilde]blāc’ is Klaeber’s: the manuscript has only ‘blāc’ and the first half is Klaeber’s addition; the apparatus lists earlier suggestions ‘heoro-’ and ‘hrēa-’, and Holthausen’s ‘hilde-’ fits the metre; ‘blāc’ means ‘pale’ (it can also mean ‘bright’), so ‘battle-pale’ is a guess at a damaged word. In ‘hond gemunde fǣhðo genōge’ the hand is taken to be Eofor’s, doing the remembering, and ‘feorhsweng ne oftēah’ is ‘did not withhold the life-stroke’ (‘oftēon’, ‘withhold’).

sentences.l: I repaid him those treasures, that he gave me, at the war, as it was granted me, with the shining sword;
sentences.i: In war I repaid him for those treasures that he gave me, as it was granted me, with my shining sword;
sentences.n: ‘Ic him … geald’ is ‘I repaid him’ (preterite of ‘gieldan’); ‘him’ is Hygelac, the king of the Geats, from whom Beowulf had had his treasure. ‘þā māðmas’ is ‘those treasures’ (accusative plural, the object of ‘geald’; ‘þā’ here is the demonstrative, not ‘then’), ‘þē hē mē sealde’ ‘that he gave me’; and ‘swā mē gifeðe wæs’ is ‘as it was granted to me’ (‘gifeðe’ is an adjective, ‘granted, given’). ‘lēohtan sweorde’ is a dative of means, ‘with the bright sword’. The reciprocity is the point: a lord’s gift is paid back in service.

sentences.t:
hē mē lond forgeaf,
eard ēðelwyn.
sentences.l: he gave me land, a dwelling, joy of the homeland.
sentences.i: He gave me land, a dwelling, the pleasure of a homeland.
sentences.n: ‘hē’ is again Hygelac, and ‘forgeaf’ ‘gave’. ‘eard ēðelwyn’ stands in apposition to ‘lond’: ‘eard’ is ‘dwelling, home’, and ‘ēðelwyn’ is ‘homeland-joy’ (‘ēðel’ ‘native land’ + ‘wyn’ ‘joy’); the apparatus records Sievers’s ‘-wynne’, which would give the word a full ending (‘-wynne’).

sentences.t:
Næs him ǣnig þearf,
þæt hē tō Gifðum oððe tō Gār-Denum
oððe in Swīorīce sēcean þurfe
wyrsan wīgfrecan, weorðe gecȳpan;
sentences.l: There was not to him any need that he need seek to the Gifthas or to the Spear-Danes or in Sweden a worse war-fighter, buy him with a price;
sentences.i: He had no need to look among the Gepids, or the Spear-Danes, or in Sweden, for a worse warrior and buy him with money;
sentences.n: ‘Næs him ǣnig þearf’ is ‘there was no need to him’, followed by a clause of what he needed not do (‘þæt hē … sēcean þurfe’, ‘that he need seek’); ‘hē’ is Hygelac. ‘wyrsan wīgfrecan’ is ‘a worse war-fighter’ (‘wīgfreca’, ‘warrior’, from ‘wīg’ ‘war’ + ‘freca’ ‘bold man’), and ‘weorðe gecȳpan’ is ‘buy with a price’ (‘weorð’ ‘worth, price’). The three names stand for ‘anywhere abroad’: ‘Gifðum’ are the Gepids, a Gothic people far off, while the Spear-Danes and the Swedes were the Geats’ neighbours. I read the point as: Hygelac had no need to hire an inferior fighter from abroad, because he had Beowulf, who served him unbought.

sentences.t:
symle ic him on fēðan beforan wolde,
āna on orde, ond swā tō aldre sceall
sæcce fremman,
sentences.l: always I would be before him in the foot-troop, alone at the point, and so for life shall I do battle,
sentences.i: I would always be in front of him in the ranks, alone at the point of the attack, and so shall I fight as long as I live,
sentences.n: ‘symle’ is ‘always’; ‘ic him on fēðan beforan wolde’ is ‘I wished to be in front of him in the foot-troop’, with the verb of being understood after ‘wolde’. ‘fēða’ is the body of foot-soldiers (here the dative ‘fēðan’), and ‘on orde’ is ‘at the point’ (‘ord’ is ‘spear-point’, hence the leading edge of a line). ‘ond swā tō aldre sceall sæcce fremman’ turns the past habit into a vow: ‘tō aldre’ is ‘for life’, ‘sæcce fremman’ ‘perform battle’.

sentences.t:
þenden þis sweord þolað,
þæt mec ǣr ond sīð oft gelǣste,
syððan ic for dugeðum Dæghrefne wearð
tō handbonan, Hūga cempan; —
sentences.l: while this sword endures, that served me early and late, often, since I before the troops became Dæghrefn’s hand-slayer, the Hugas’ champion; —
sentences.i: for as long as this sword holds out, which has served me early and late, many a time, ever since I killed Dæghrefn with my own hands before the host, the champion of the Hugas; —
sentences.n: ‘þenden’ is ‘while’, and ‘þolað’ ‘endures’. ‘þæt’ is the relative, ‘which’, referring to ‘sweord’, and ‘gelǣste’ the preterite of ‘gelǣstan’, ‘perform, serve’; ‘ǣr ond sīð’ is ‘early and late’. ‘tō handbonan’ is ‘as hand-slayer’ (‘handbona’), a killer by his own hand; the lines below show it was by grip, not blade. ‘for dugeðum’ is ‘before the troops’ (‘duguð’ ‘the seasoned warriors’). The Hugas are the Franks (‘Hūga’ genitive plural). Dæghrefn is named only here; the Frisian king in the next lines ties his death to the Frisian campaign in which Hygelac fell (2354–2359), which is the usual reading but is inference, not stated outright. The apparatus notes that Grein, Schücking and Sedgefield put the full stop after ‘gelǣste’. The dash is Klaeber’s, marking the turn to the next sentence.

sentences.t:
nalles hē ðā frætwe Frēscyning[e],
brēostweorðunge bringan mōste,
ac in campe gecrong cumbles hyrde,
æþeling on elne;
sentences.l: not at all was he allowed to bring those ornaments to the Frisian king, the breast-adornment, but in the fight fell the keeper of the standard, the atheling in courage;
sentences.i: He was not allowed to bring those ornaments, the breast-finery, to the Frisian king; the keeper of the standard fell in the fight, the prince, fighting bravely;
sentences.n: ‘nalles’ is ‘not at all’, ‘mōste’ ‘was allowed’. ‘Frēscyning[e]’ is the dative, ‘to the Frisian king’; the manuscript has ‘cyning’ and the bracketed ‘e’ is Grundtvig’s ending, which the grammar requires. ‘brēostweorðunge’ is ‘breast-adornment’ (‘brēost’ ‘breast’ + ‘weorðung’ ‘adornment’), a piece of treasure worn on the breast, probably what Dæghrefn took from the fallen Geats; the poem does not say whose it was. Klaeber’s italic ‘a’ and ‘e’ in ‘campe’ mark an alteration: the manuscript has ‘cempan’, ‘warriors’, and Kemble’s ‘campe’ (‘camp’, ‘battle’, borrowed from Latin ‘campus’) makes ‘in the fight’. ‘cumbles hyrde’ is ‘keeper of the standard’ (‘cumbol’ ‘banner’), so Dæghrefn was the Frankish standard-bearer; Beowulf, who is speaking, gives the dead man his title. ‘æþeling on elne’ is ‘a prince in courage’.

sentences.t:
ne wæs ecg bona,
ac him hildegrāp heortan wylmas,
bānhūs gebræc.
sentences.l: no sword-edge was the slayer, but battle-grip broke for him the heart’s surgings, the bone-house.
sentences.i: No sword’s edge was his slayer: it was the grip of battle that crushed the surging of his heart, the very frame of his body.
sentences.n: ‘ne wæs ecg bona’ is ‘the edge was not the slayer’ (‘bona’ ‘slayer’). ‘ac him hildegrāp heortan wylmas, bānhūs gebræc’ is ‘but battle-grip broke for him the heart’s surges, the bone-house’. ‘hildegrāp’ is ‘battle-grip’ (‘hild’ ‘battle’ + ‘grāp’ ‘grip’), the subject; ‘heortan wylmas’ (‘surgings of the heart’) and ‘bānhūs’ (‘bone-house’, the chest or body) are the objects, in apposition. So Beowulf killed him by his grip. ‘bānhūs’ is a house-kenning for the body, like ‘bāncofa’.

sentences.t:
Nū sceall billes ecg,
hond ond heard sweord ymb hord wīgan.’
sentences.l: Now shall the edge of the blade, the hand and the hard sword, fight for the hoard.’
sentences.i: Now the edge of the blade, my hand and my hard sword, shall fight for the hoard.’
sentences.n: ‘Nū sceall’ is ‘now shall’, with ‘wīgan’ (‘fight’) at the end of the sentence; the subject is three things in a row, ‘billes ecg, hond ond heard sweord’ (‘the edge of the blade, the hand and the hard sword’), the verb ‘sceall’ is singular although the subject is a list. The apparatus records Morgan’s and Holthausen’s reading of ‘heard sweord’ as one word, ‘heardsweord’. ‘ymb hord’ is ‘about the hoard’. The closing quotation mark ends the long speech that began in the previous Fitt.

sentences.t:
Bēowulf maðelode, bēotwordum spræc
nīehstan sīðe:
sentences.l: Beowulf spoke in speech-words, spoke with vow-words for the last time:
sentences.i: Beowulf spoke in formal words, spoke words of vowing for the last time:
sentences.n: ‘Bēowulf maðelode’ is the poem’s regular introduction of a formal speech (‘spoke in speech-words’, the house rendering for this verb). ‘bēotwordum’ is ‘with vow-words’ (‘bēot’ ‘vow, boast’ + ‘word’ ‘word’): a ‘bēot’ is a public promise of a deed, made before witnesses and owed afterwards. ‘nīehstan sīðe’ is a dative of time, ‘for the nearest/last time’ (‘nīehsta’ is the superlative of ‘nēah’); the poet marks this as the last time Beowulf is said to speak vow-words.

sentences.t:
‘Ic genēðde fela
gūða on geogoðe;
sentences.l: ‘I ventured many battles in youth;
sentences.i: ‘In my youth I dared many battles;
sentences.n: ‘genēðde’ is the preterite of ‘genēðan’, ‘venture, dare’, and ‘fela gūða’ ‘many of battles’, with ‘fela’ taking a genitive plural. ‘on geogoðe’ is ‘in youth’. ‘Ic’ is the subject and ‘fela’ the object, a neuter noun taking the genitive plural ‘gūða’.

sentences.t:
gȳt ic wylle,
frōd folces weard fǣhðe sēcan,
mǣrðu fremman, gif mec se mānsceaða
of eorðsele ūt gesēceð.’
sentences.l: yet will I, wise guardian of the people, seek the feud, do deeds of glory, if the crime-scather out of the earth-hall seeks me out.’
sentences.i: yet, old guardian of the people, I will still seek out the feud and do deeds of glory, if the wicked marauder comes out of his earth-hall to find me.’
sentences.n: ‘gȳt ic wylle’ is ‘still I will’; ‘frōd folces weard’ is ‘wise guardian of the people’ (‘frōd’ ‘wise, old’), Beowulf as king. ‘fǣhðe sēcan’ is ‘seek the feud’, to go looking for the fight, and ‘mǣrðu fremman’ ‘do glorious deeds’. Klaeber’s italic ‘u’ in ‘mǣrðu’ marks an alteration: the apparatus gives the manuscript ending as ‘mærðū’, where the macron stands for ‘m’ (so ‘mǣrðum’), and ‘mǣrðu’ is the accusative plural read by Bugge and three editors (Kemble read ‘mǣrðo’). ‘mānsceaða’ is ‘crime-scather’, the house term for the dragon (as for Grendel), and ‘eorðsele’ the ‘earth-hall’ of the barrow. ‘gif … gesēceð’ is a condition in the present tense: if he seeks me out (‘ūt’ ‘out’) from the earth-hall.

sentences.t:
Gegrētte ðā gumena gehwylcne,
hwate helmberend hindeman sīðe,
swǣse gesīðas:
sentences.l: He greeted then each of the men, the bold helmet-bearers, for the last time, the dear companions:
sentences.i: Then he greeted each of his men, those bold helmet-wearers, for the last time, his dear companions:
sentences.n: ‘Gegrētte’ is ‘greeted’, with the subject Beowulf understood, and ‘gumena gehwylcne’ ‘each of the men’; ‘hwate helmberend’ and ‘swǣse gesīðas’ are variations on the same men, ‘bold helmet-bearers’ and ‘dear companions’. ‘helmberend’ is ‘helmet-bearers’ (‘helm’ + ‘berend’ ‘bearer’), a common word for warriors. ‘hindeman sīðe’ is ‘for the last time’, a dative like ‘nīehstan sīðe’ above. The poet has now marked ‘the last time’ twice in a few lines.

sentences.t:
‘Nolde ic sweord beran,
wǣpen tō wyrme, gif ic wiste hū
wið ðām āglǣcean elles meahte
gylpe wiðgrīpan, swā ic giō wið Grendle dyde;
sentences.l: ‘I would not bear a sword, a weapon against the worm, if I knew how otherwise I could grapple with the awesome one in boast, as I once did against Grendel;
sentences.i: ‘I would not carry a sword, or any weapon, against the dragon, if I knew how else I could grapple with this fearsome creature and make good my vow, as I did with Grendel long ago;
sentences.n: ‘Nolde’ is ‘ne wolde’, ‘would not’, and the condition ‘gif ic wiste hū … elles meahte’ is ‘if I knew how … I otherwise could’: he would rather wrestle, as he did with Grendel, but this foe cannot be wrestled. ‘wyrme’ is the dative of ‘wyrm’ (‘worm’, ‘dragon’), and ‘āglǣcean’ the dative of ‘āglǣca’, ‘awesome one’; the lexica cannot settle the word’s root, and the poem applies it to Grendel, to Grendel’s mother, to the dragon, and (below, 2592) to Beowulf himself. ‘gylpe wiðgrīpan’ is the hard phrase: ‘wiðgrīpan’ is ‘grapple with’ and ‘gylp’ ‘boast’, and I take the dative as ‘in boast’, meaning ‘to make good the vow’; this is a reading. The apparatus gives Schröer’s ‘gūþe’ (‘in war’) as a way to avoid the problem. ‘giō’ is ‘formerly’.

sentences.t:
ac ic ðǣr heaðufȳres hātes wēne,
[o]reðes ond attres; forðon ic mē on hafu
bord ond byrnan.
sentences.l: but I there expect hot battle-fire, breath and venom; therefore I have on me shield and byrnie.
sentences.i: But there I expect hot fire of battle, breath and poison; so I have shield and mail-coat on me.
sentences.n: ‘wēne’ is ‘expect’ (‘wēnan’), taking a genitive, ‘heaðufȳres hātes … oreðes ond attres’, ‘of hot battle-fire, of breath and of venom’. The brackets in ‘[o]reðes’ are Grein’s: the apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘reðes’, which is ‘oreðes’ without its first letter. Klaeber’s italic ‘a’ in ‘attres’ marks another alteration: the manuscript has ‘hattres’ (written ‘⁊ hattres’, ‘and hattres’), and Grundtvig and Kemble dropped the ‘h’ to give ‘atter’ (‘ator’ ‘poison, venom’). ‘forðon’ is ‘therefore’ and ‘on hafu’ ‘have on me’. ‘bord ond byrnan’ (‘shield and byrnie’) are the defences he has put on against that fire and poison.

sentences.t:
Nelle ic beorges weard
oferfleôn fōtes trem, ac unc [furður] sceal
weorðan æt wealle, swā unc wyrd getēoð,
Metod manna gehwæs.
sentences.l: I will not flee a foot’s pace from the barrow’s guardian, but [further] for us two it shall come to be at the wall, as fate assigns us, the Measurer of each man.
sentences.i: I will not flee a single step from the guardian of the barrow; but what further befalls the two of us at the wall shall be as fate decrees, as the Measurer decides for every man.
sentences.n: ‘Nelle’ is ‘ne wille’, ‘will not’; ‘oferfleôn’, with a circumflex for the contracted vowel (the manuscript has ‘ofer fleon’, which the apparatus shows editors dividing differently), is ‘flee from’, with the object ‘beorges weard’ (‘the barrow’s guardian’); ‘fōtes trem’ is ‘a foot’s step’. ‘unc’ is the dual pronoun, ‘us two’: Beowulf and the dragon. The bracket in ‘[furður]’ is Klaeber’s: the manuscript line has no word there; Schubert, Barnouw and Trautmann supplied ‘[fǣhðo]’, Bugge and Schücking ‘[feohte]’, and ‘[furður]’ (‘further’) is Chambers’s (the Archiv has ‘furðor’), so the sense ‘further’ is a guess. ‘swā unc wyrd getēoð’ is ‘as fate assigns to us’ (‘getēon’ ‘ordain, assign’), and ‘Metod manna gehwæs’ ‘the Measurer of each man’ (‘Metod’ is God as the one who measures out), named beside ‘wyrd’ as the power behind it.

sentences.t:
Ic eom on mōde from,
þæt ic wið þone gūðflogan gylp ofersitte.
sentences.l: I am bold in mind, so that I forgo boast against the war-flier.
sentences.i: I am bold of heart, and will say no more boastful words against this flyer of war.
sentences.n: ‘from’ here is an adjective, ‘bold, strong’ (the same word as in ‘frome fyrdhwate’ above), and ‘on mōde’ ‘in mind, in spirit’. ‘þæt … ofersitte’ is a result clause: ‘ofersittan’ is ‘sit over, omit’, so ‘gylp ofersitte’ is ‘forgo boasting’. The apparatus notes Sievers’s ‘þæs’ for ‘þæt’. ‘gūðflogan’ is ‘war-flier’ (‘gūð’ ‘war’ + ‘floga’ ‘flier’), the dragon. The speech has just been a boast, so ‘no more’ closes it: from here he fights.

sentences.t:
Gebīde gē on beorge byrnum werede,
secgas on searwum, hwæðer sēl mæge
æfter wælrǣse wunde gedȳgan
uncer twēga.
sentences.l: Wait you on the barrow, covered in byrnies, men in armour, which of us can better survive the wound after the slaughter-rush, of us two.
sentences.i: Wait on the barrow, you men in your armour and mail, to see which of us two can better come through his wounds after the onslaught.
sentences.n: ‘Gebīde’ is a plural imperative, ‘wait’ (‘gebīdan’), with ‘gē’ ‘you’ written out. ‘byrnum werede’ is ‘clad in byrnies’ (‘werede’ past participle of ‘werian’ ‘clothe’), ‘secgas on searwum’ ‘men in armour’, both variations on the plural subject. ‘hwæðer sēl mæge … gedȳgan’ is an indirect question, ‘which can better survive’, and ‘wunde’ is the object of ‘gedȳgan’, ‘come through the wound’; ‘wælrǣse’ is ‘slaughter-rush’ (‘wæl’ ‘slaughter’ + ‘rǣs’ ‘rush’). ‘uncer twēga’ is a genitive dual, ‘of us two’. The men are told to wait and watch.

sentences.t:
Nis þæt ēower sīð,
nē gemet mannes, nefn(e) mīn ānes,
þæt hē wið āglǣcean eofoðo dǣle,
eorlscype efne.
sentences.l: It is not your venture, nor a man’s measure, except mine alone, that he should deal strength against the awesome one, perform an earl’s deed.
sentences.i: This is no venture for you, nor within any man’s measure but mine alone, to match strength with this fearsome creature and do an earl’s deed.
sentences.n: ‘Nis’ is ‘ne is’, ‘is not’, and the subject is the whole ‘þæt hē … dǣle, … efne’ clause: ‘that he should … deal out … perform’, with ‘hē’ any man. ‘ēower sīð’ is ‘your venture’; ‘gemet mannes’ is ‘a man’s measure’ (what a man is fit for). ‘nefn(e)’ is ‘nemne’, ‘except, unless’, with the parenthesis Klaeber’s sign that the final letter is restored (the apparatus credits Grundtvig’s translation). Klaeber’s italic ‘þæ’ in ‘þæt’ marks an alteration; the apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘wat’. ‘eofoðo’ is ‘strength, violence’, and ‘eorlscype’ ‘earl’s deed, manliness’. The sentence uses a general statement (‘no man’) to claim the fight for himself.

sentences.t:
Ic mid elne sceall
gold gegangan, oððe gūð nimeð,
feorhbealu frēcne frēan ēowerne!’
sentences.l: I with courage shall win the gold, or war will take, fierce life-bale, your lord!’
sentences.i: I shall win the gold by courage, or else battle will take your lord, fierce life-bale!’
sentences.n: ‘gold gegangan’ is ‘gain the gold’ (‘gegangan’ ‘get by going’), ‘mid elne’ ‘with courage’. ‘oððe gūð nimeð’ is ‘or war will take’, and the two subjects, ‘gūð’ and ‘feorhbealu frēcne’ (‘fierce life-bale’, ‘feorh’ ‘life’ + ‘bealu’ ‘bale’), share the object ‘frēan ēowerne’, ‘your lord’, in the accusative. The bluntness of ‘your lord’ is Beowulf describing his own death in the third person.

sentences.t:
Ārās ðā bī ronde rōf ōretta,
heard under helme, hiorosercean bær
under stāncleofu, strengo getrūwọde
ānes mannes;
sentences.l: Rose then by his shield the brave warrior, hard under helm, bore the sword-shirt under the stone-cliffs, trusted in the strength of one man;
sentences.i: Then the stout champion rose by his shield, hard under his helmet, and carried his mail-shirt under the stone cliffs, trusting in the strength of one man alone;
sentences.n: ‘Ārās’ is ‘rose’; ‘bī ronde’ is ‘by his shield’ (‘rond’ ‘shield’); ‘rōf ōretta’ is ‘brave champion’ (‘ōretta’, a poetic word for a warrior). ‘hiorosercean’ is ‘sword-shirt’ (‘hioro’ ‘sword’ + ‘serce’ ‘shirt’), a mail-coat, the object of ‘bær’ (‘bore’); ‘under stāncleofu’ is ‘under the stone cliffs’, the rocky cliffs by the barrow. ‘strengo getrūwọde ānes mannes’ is ‘trusted in the strength of one man’ (‘strengo’ is the object of trust, and ‘ānes mannes’ its genitive, ‘of one man’): his only help is himself. The dot under the ‘ọ’ in ‘getrūwọde’ is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre, so the word scans as if the vowel were absent; it changes nothing in the sense, and ‘dōgọre’ (2573) and ‘hrēoụm’ (2581) have others in this part.

sentences.t: ne bið swylc earges sīð!
sentences.l: not such is a coward’s venture!
sentences.i: A coward’s errand is not like this!
sentences.n: A poet’s comment in the present tense (‘bið’, the general present of ‘bēon’): ‘ne bið swylc earges sīð’ is ‘such is not a coward’s journey’, meaning that a coward does not do this. ‘earges’ is the genitive of the adjective ‘earg’, ‘cowardly’, used as a noun, ‘of a coward’. Klaeber’s exclamation mark marks the poet’s voice as an aside before the fight.

sentences.t:
Geseah ðā be wealle sē ðe worna fela
gumcystum gōd gūða gedīgde,
hildehlemma, þonne hnitan fēðan,
sto[n]dan stānbogan, strēam ūt þonan
brecan of beorge;
sentences.l: Saw then by the wall he who, good in manly virtues, had come through very many wars, clashes of battle, when foot-troops struck together, stone arches stand, a stream break out from the barrow;
sentences.i: Then he who was so excellent in manly virtue, and had come through so many wars and clashes of battle when armies met, saw by the wall stone arches standing, and a stream bursting out from the mound;
sentences.n: The long sentence runs in two parts: ‘Geseah ðā be wealle sē ðe …’ (‘saw then by the wall he who …’), where ‘sē ðe’ is Beowulf, and then the two things he saw, ‘stānbogan’ standing and a ‘strēam’ breaking out. ‘gumcystum gōd’ is ‘good in manly virtues’ (‘gum’ ‘man’ + ‘cyst’ ‘excellence’); ‘gūða gedīgde’ ‘came through wars’ (‘gedīgan’ ‘survive’, the same verb as at 2531). ‘hildehlemma’ is ‘battle-crashes’, genitive plural, and ‘worna fela’ ‘very many’. ‘hnitan’ is ‘clashed, struck together’ (preterite plural of ‘hnītan’), ‘fēðan’ ‘foot-troops’. The bracket in ‘sto[n]dan’ is Thorpe’s: the manuscript has ‘stodan’, and the ‘n’ is added. ‘stānbogan’ is ‘stone arches’, presumably the rock vault at the barrow’s mouth; the poem does not describe it further.

sentences.t:
wæs þǣre burnan wælm
heaðofȳrum hāt; ne meahte horde nēah
unbyrnende ǣnige hwīle
dēop gedȳgan for dracan lēge.
sentences.l: the surge of that stream was hot with battle-fires; no one could near the hoard unburning any while survive in the deep because of the dragon’s flame.
sentences.i: The surge of that stream was hot with fires of battle; no one could survive for any time in its depths near the hoard without being burned, because of the dragon’s flame.
sentences.n: ‘wæs þǣre burnan wælm … hāt’ is ‘the surge of that stream was hot’, with ‘heaðofȳrum’ a dative of cause, ‘with battle-fires’. In ‘ne meahte … gedȳgan’ the subject is understood, ‘no one’, and ‘unbyrnende’ is ‘unburning’, the poet’s word for ‘without being burnt’. ‘dēop’ is a noun, ‘the deep’; the apparatus records ‘dēor’ in Grundtvig (as a noun, ‘animal’) and in Bugge and Sedgefield (as an adjective, ‘bold’), which would read ‘no bold man could survive’. ‘for dracan lēge’ is ‘because of the dragon’s flame’. The stream comes from under the barrow, heated by the creature inside.

sentences.l: Let then from his breast, when he was swollen with rage, the man of the Weder-Geats words go out, stout-hearted he stormed;
sentences.i: Then, enraged, the prince of the Geats let words burst from his breast; he shouted with a stern heart;
sentences.n: ‘Lēt … faran’ is ‘let go’ (‘lǣtan’ with an infinitive), with ‘word ūt’ the object: he shouted a challenge. ‘ðā hē gebolgen wæs’ is ‘when he was swollen’ with anger, the usual verb for rage in the poem. ‘Weder-Gēata lēod’ is ‘man (prince) of the Weder-Geats’, Beowulf. ‘stearcheort’ is ‘stern-hearted’ (‘stearc’ ‘stern’ + ‘heort’ ‘heart’), ‘styrmde’ ‘stormed, shouted’. What he shouted is not given; the next words show it echoing in the barrow.

sentences.t:
stefn in becōm
heaðotorht hlynnan under hārne stān.
sentences.l: a voice came in, battle-bright, ringing under the hoar stone.
sentences.i: His voice, battle-clear, went in and rang beneath the grey stone.
sentences.n: ‘stefn’ is ‘voice’ (the word also means ‘time, turn’, as in ‘nīwan stefne’ below); ‘becōm’ is ‘came to’ and ‘in’ the direction. ‘heaðotorht’ is ‘battle-bright’ (‘heaðo’ ‘battle’ + ‘torht’ ‘bright, clear’), here ‘clear and ringing’. ‘hlynnan’ I take as an infinitive ‘to resound’; the verb is rare and the sense is partly a guess. ‘hārne stān’ is ‘hoar stone’ (‘hār’ ‘grey with age’), the rock of the barrow.

sentences.t:
Hete wæs onhrēred, hordweard oncnīow
mannes reorde;
sentences.l: Hate was stirred up; the hoard-guard knew a man’s speech;
sentences.i: Hostility was roused; the guardian of the hoard knew the voice of a man;
sentences.n: ‘Hete’ is the noun ‘hate’, the subject of ‘wæs onhrēred’, ‘was stirred up’ (past participle of ‘onhrēran’). ‘hordweard’ is ‘hoard-guard’, and ‘oncnīow’ is the preterite of ‘oncnāwan’, ‘recognise, know’; ‘mannes reorde’ is ‘a man’s voice’ (‘reord’ ‘speech, voice’).

sentences.t:
næs ðǣr māra fyrst
frēode tō friclan.
sentences.l: there was no more respite to seek peace.
sentences.i: There was no longer time to ask for peace.
sentences.n: ‘næs’ is ‘ne wæs’, ‘was not’; ‘māra fyrst’ is ‘more time’ (‘fyrst’ ‘period, respite’); ‘frēode tō friclan’ is ‘to seek peace’. The verb ‘friclan’ occurs nowhere else, and I take ‘seek, desire’ from the lexica; the sense is a guess, but the context needs something like it. The shout has roused the dragon, and the time for any parley is over.

sentences.t:
From ǣrest cwōm
oruð āglǣcean ūt of stāne,
hāt hildeswāt; hrūse dynede.
sentences.l: Forth first came the breath of the awesome one out of the stone, hot battle-sweat; the earth resounded.
sentences.i: First came the breath of the fearsome creature, bursting out of the rock, hot with the sweat of battle; the ground rang.
sentences.n: ‘From’ is the adjective ‘bold’ at 2527; here I read it as the adverb ‘forth, forward’, which is a judgement, and ‘ǣrest’ is ‘first’. ‘oruð’ is ‘breath’, the same word as ‘oreð’ in ‘[o]reðes’ at 2523. ‘hāt hildeswāt’ is ‘hot battle-sweat’ (‘hild’ ‘battle’ + ‘swāt’ ‘sweat’; compare ‘heaþoswāt’ earlier in the poem), in apposition to ‘oruð’: the steam or fire that comes out. ‘hrūse dynede’ is ‘the earth resounded’ (‘dynian’), ‘hrūse’ is the nominative subject.

sentences.t:
Biorn under beorge bordrand onswāf
wið ðām gryregieste, Gēata dryhten;
sentences.l: The man under the barrow swung his shield-rim against the terror-guest, the lord of the Geats;
sentences.i: The man beneath the barrow swung his shield’s rim against the dread visitor, the lord of the Geats;
sentences.n: ‘Biorn’ is the poetic ‘beorn’, ‘man, warrior’, Beowulf; the apparatus records Sedgefield’s ‘born’, which would be a verb ‘burned’ and shift the punctuation. ‘bordrand’ is ‘shield-rim’ (a poetic word for the shield), the object of ‘onswāf’, which I take as ‘swung’ (the lexica give ‘swing’ for ‘onswīfan’) and which is not otherwise used, so this is partly a guess. ‘wið ðām gryregieste’ is ‘against the terror-guest’ (‘gryre’ ‘terror’ + ‘giest’ ‘guest, stranger’), the dragon; ‘Gēata dryhten’ ‘lord of the Geats’ stands in apposition to ‘Biorn’.

sentences.t:
ðā wæs hringbogan heorte gefȳsed
sæcce tō sēceanne.
sentences.l: Then was the heart of the ring-bowed one impelled to seek the battle.
sentences.i: Then the heart of the coiled creature was stirred to seek the fight.
sentences.n: ‘ðā wæs … heorte gefȳsed’ is ‘then was the heart impelled’ (‘gefȳsed’ past participle of ‘fȳsan’, ‘drive forward’). ‘hringbogan’ is ‘ring-bowed’ (‘hring’ ‘ring’ + ‘boga’ ‘bow, bend’), a coiled serpent; I read it as the dragon. The apparatus records Sarrazin’s ‘hringboran’ (‘ring-bearer’), which would make the subject Beowulf; the whole thing turns on the one letter. ‘sæcce tō sēceanne’ is ‘to seek battle’ (‘sēceanne’ the inflected infinitive; Sievers, Holthausen and others print ‘sēc(e)an’).

sentences.l: Earlier the good war-king drew the sword, an old legacy, un-dull in its edges;
sentences.i: The good war-king had already drawn his sword, an old heirloom, keen in its edges;
sentences.n: ‘gebrǣd’ is the preterite of ‘bregdan’, ‘draw’, with ‘ǣr’ ‘earlier’ (already, before this), ‘gōd gūðcyning’ the subject (‘war-king’, Beowulf) and ‘sweord’ the object put first. ‘gomele lāfe’ is ‘old legacy’ (‘lāf’ ‘what is left, heirloom’), in apposition. The last word is a crux: Klaeber prints ‘anglāw’ with the italic ‘a’, and the apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘unglaw’ (‘un/glaw’, with a letter erased after the ‘l’) and records Thorpe’s ‘unslēaw’ and Bugge’s and four editors’ ‘unslāw’, ‘not blunt’. Klaeber’s ‘anglāw’ is not a word the lexica list, and I render the sense of ‘unslāw’, ‘not dull’, as a guess.

sentences.t:
ǣghwæðrum wæs
bealohycgendra brōga fram ōðrum.
sentences.l: to each of the baleful-minded ones there was terror from the other.
sentences.i: Each of the two, bent on harm, was terrified of the other.
sentences.n: ‘ǣghwæðrum’ is a dative, ‘to each of the two’, and ‘bealohycgendra’ a genitive plural, ‘of the harm-planners’ (‘bealu’ ‘harm’ + ‘hycgan’ ‘think, intend’), the pair of fighters. ‘brōga fram ōðrum’ is ‘terror from the other’. Each is afraid of the other, man and dragon alike.

sentences.t:
Stīðmōd gestōd wið stēapne rond
winia bealdor, ðā se wyrm gebēah
snūde tōsomne; hē on searwum bād.
sentences.l: Stern-minded stood against the steep shield the prince of friends, when the worm coiled quickly together; he in armour waited.
sentences.i: Resolute, the lord of his friends stood against his tall shield as the dragon bent itself swiftly together; he waited in his armour.
sentences.n: ‘Stīðmōd’ is ‘stern-minded’, ‘gestōd’ ‘stood’, ‘wið stēapne rond’ ‘against the high shield’. ‘winia bealdor’ is ‘lord (prince) of friends’ (‘bealdor’ ‘lord, prince’, related to ‘beald’ ‘bold’; ‘winia’ genitive plural of ‘wine’ ‘friend’): Beowulf. The apparatus records Grundtvig’s ‘wigena’, ‘of warriors’. ‘gebēah … tōsomne’ is ‘bent together’, the dragon coiling to spring, and ‘snūde’ ‘swiftly’. ‘hē on searwum bād’ is ‘he waited in armour’, where ‘bād’ is the preterite of ‘bīdan’.

sentences.t:
Gewāt ðā byrnende gebogen scrīðan,
tō gescipe scyndan.
sentences.l: Went then, burning, bent, gliding, to its fate hastening.
sentences.i: Then, burning and bent, it came gliding, hastening to its fate.
sentences.n: ‘Gewāt … scrīðan’ is ‘went gliding’, the infinitive of manner; ‘byrnende gebogen’ is ‘burning, coiled’, two participles for the fiery serpent. ‘tō gescipe scyndan’ is ‘hasten to its fate’, where ‘gescipe’ is a word of doubtful form: the apparatus lists Thorpe’s ‘gesceape’, Ettmüller’s ‘gescepe’, and the readings ‘gescīfe’ (‘headlong’, with ‘tō’ moved back to the previous line) of Heyne’s later editions and Holthausen. I take ‘fate’ because it matches the sense of ‘gesceap’, and mark it as a guess.

sentences.l: The shield protected well life and body for a lesser while the famed prince, than his desire sought;
sentences.i: The shield protected the famed prince’s life and body well, but for a shorter time than he had hoped;
sentences.n: ‘Scyld wēl gebearg’ is ‘the shield protected well’ (‘gebearg’ preterite of ‘gebeorgan’, with datives ‘līfe ond līce’, ‘for life and body’, and ‘mǣrum þēodne’, ‘for the famed prince’). ‘lǣssan hwīle’ is ‘for a lesser while’, and ‘þonne his myne sōhte’ ‘than his purpose sought’, which I read as ‘than he had expected or wished’; ‘myne’ is ‘mind, desire’, and the whole clause is hard to be sure of. The poet says in advance that the shield fails, which prepares the sword’s failing too.

sentences.t:
ðǣr hē þȳ fyrste forman dōgọre
wealdan mōste, swā him wyrd ne gescrāf
hrēð æt hilde.
sentences.l: where he for that time on the first day might have the mastery, as fate had not allotted him glory in the fight.
sentences.i: There, on that first day, he was allowed the mastery for a time, though fate had not allotted him glory in the fight.
sentences.n: The construction is difficult. ‘ðǣr’ (‘where, in which case’) opens a clause on ‘wealdan mōste’, ‘might (was to) rule’; ‘þȳ fyrste forman dōgọre’ is ‘at that time, on the first day’ (the apparatus refers to 1797, which has the same ‘þȳ … dōgọre’). ‘swā him wyrd ne gescrāf’ is ‘as fate did not allot him’ (‘gescrīfan’ ‘decree, assign’), with ‘hrēð’ ‘glory, triumph’ and ‘æt hilde’ ‘in battle’. I read it as: the shield protected him for a time in which he was to prevail, but fate had not decreed the victory. This is my best reading of a disputed passage. The dot under the ‘ọ’ of ‘dōgọre’ is the metrical sign explained at 2540.

sentences.t:
Hond ūp ābrǣd
Gēata dryhten, gryrefāhne slōh
incge-lāfe,
sentences.l: Hand up swung the lord of the Geats, struck the terror-coloured one with the Incge-legacy,
sentences.i: The lord of the Geats raised his hand and struck the dread-hued creature with the heirloom sword,
sentences.n: ‘Hond ūp ābrǣd’ is ‘raised his hand up’ (‘ābregdan’, ‘lift, swing’), ‘Gēata dryhten’ the subject. ‘gryrefāhne’ is ‘terror-coloured’ (‘gryre’ ‘terror’ + ‘fāh’ ‘coloured, stained’), the dragon with its terrible markings, in the accusative. ‘incge-lāfe’ is the instrument, ‘with the Incge-legacy’, and the hyphen marks ‘incge’ as the first element of a compound of uncertain meaning. The apparatus lists many readings: Kemble’s ‘īcge-’, ‘Incges’ in Thorpe, Ettmüller and Sedgefield (‘of Incg’), Grundtvig’s ‘Ingwina’ (queried), Holthausen’s ‘Ingwines’, Trautmann’s ‘isigre’. The likeliest sense is ‘an heirloom of Incg’, an owner or maker of the sword whom nothing else names; I render ‘heirloom’ and treat the first half of the word as a guess.

sentences.t:
þæt sīo ecg gewāc
brūn on bāne, bāt unswīðor,
þonne his ðīodcyning þearfe hæfde
bysigum gebǣded.
sentences.l: so that the edge gave way, brown on the bone, bit less strongly than its people-king had need, pressed by troubles.
sentences.i: so that the burnished edge failed on the bone, and bit less keenly than its prince, hard pressed in his need, required.
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ introduces the result: ‘sīo ecg gewāc’, ‘the edge gave way’ (‘gewīcan’, ‘yield’). ‘brūn’ is ‘brown’, probably of burnished, dark-shining metal, and ‘on bāne’ ‘on the bone’. ‘bāt unswīðor’ is ‘bit less strongly’, and ‘þonne’ ‘than’. ‘his ðīodcyning’ is ‘its people-king’, the prince who owned it, and ‘þearfe hæfde bysigum gebǣded’ ‘had need, pressed by troubles’ (‘gebǣdan’ ‘press hard’). The sword fails exactly when the king needs it most.

sentences.l: Then was the barrow’s guardian after the battle-blow in a fierce mood, flung slaughter-fire;
sentences.i: Then, after the blow, the guardian of the barrow was in a savage temper and flung out deadly fire;
sentences.n: ‘Þā wæs … on hrēoụm mōde’ is ‘then was … in a savage mood’ (‘hrēoh’ ‘rough, fierce’, a dative here). The dot under the ‘ụ’ in ‘hrēoụm’ is the same metrical sign as in ‘getrūwọde’. ‘beorges weard’ is ‘the barrow’s guardian’, the dragon; ‘heaðuswenge’ is ‘battle-blow’; ‘wearp wælfȳre’ is ‘flung slaughter-fire’ (‘weorpan’ ‘throw’).

sentences.t:
wīde sprungon
hildelēoman.
sentences.l: far and wide sprang the battle-lights.
sentences.i: Far and wide the flames of battle leapt.
sentences.n: ‘hildelēoman’ is ‘battle-lights’ (‘hild’ ‘battle’ + ‘lēoma’ ‘ray, flame’; compare ‘beadolēoma’), the sparks and flames that the fire flings. ‘wīde sprungon’ is ‘sprang widely’. The sentence is the dragon’s breath again, now with the fight fully on.

sentences.t:
Hrēðsigora ne gealp
goldwine Gēata; gūðbill geswāc
nacod æt nīðe, swā hyt nō sceolde,
īren ǣrgōd. —
sentences.l: Of glory-victories the gold-friend of the Geats did not boast; the war-bill failed, naked at the fight, as it should not have, the iron good of old. —
sentences.i: The gold-friend of the Geats had no triumph to boast of; his war-blade failed him, bare in the fight, as it never should have, that iron once so good. —
sentences.n: ‘ne gealp’ is ‘did not boast’ (‘gielpan’, here with a genitive: ‘Hrēðsigora’, ‘of glory-victories’ from ‘hrēð’ ‘glory’ + ‘sige’ ‘victory’). ‘goldwine Gēata’ is ‘gold-friend of the Geats’ (‘goldwine’, a title for a generous lord), ‘gūðbill’ ‘war-bill’, a sword, and ‘geswāc’ the preterite of ‘geswīcan’, ‘fail’. ‘nacod’ is ‘naked’, with the sense ‘bare, unsheathed’. ‘swā hyt nō sceolde’ is ‘as it ought not’, and ‘īren ǣrgōd’ ‘iron, good from of old’ in apposition. Klaeber’s dash sets off what follows as the poet’s aside.

sentences.l: That was not an easy journey, that the famed son of Ecgtheow would give up that ground-plain;
sentences.i: It was no easy journey, that the famed son of Ecgtheow was to give up that plain of earth;
sentences.n: ‘Ne wæs þæt ēðe sīð’ is ‘that was no easy journey’, with ‘þæt … wolde’ explaining what the journey was. ‘maga Ecgðēowes’ is ‘son of Ecgtheow’ (‘maga’ ‘son’), Beowulf. ‘grundwong’ is ‘ground-plain’ (‘grund’ ‘ground’ + ‘wong’ ‘field’), the earth itself. ‘ofgyfan’ is ‘give up’, and the poet is saying that Beowulf was going to die.

sentences.t:
sceolde [ofer] willan wīc eardian
elles hwergen, swā sceal ǣghwylc mon
ālǣtan lǣndagas.
sentences.l: he had to against his will inhabit a dwelling elsewhere somewhere, as each man must leave the lent days.
sentences.i: He had to take up his dwelling, against his will, somewhere else, as every man must give up the days lent to him.
sentences.n: ‘sceolde … wīc eardian’ is ‘had to inhabit a dwelling’, ‘elles hwergen’ ‘somewhere else’, which is a euphemism for dying and for wherever the dead go. The bracket in ‘[ofer]’ is Rieger’s and four editors’: the manuscript lacks the word, and with ‘ofer willan’ the phrase is ‘against his will’; the apparatus lists Grein’s ‘[wyrmes]’ (‘the worm’s dwelling’) and the proposal ‘[wyrme tō]’, which would put the dwelling at ‘the worm’s will’. ‘lǣndagas’ is ‘lent days’ (‘lǣn’ ‘loan’ + ‘dagas’ ‘days’), the days of life seen as lent to a man. ‘swā sceal ǣghwylc mon’ is ‘as every man must’, a general truth.

sentences.t:
Næs ðā long tō ðon,
þæt ðā āglǣcean hȳ eft gemētton.
sentences.l: It was not long until then, that the awesome ones, they, met again.
sentences.i: It was not long before the two fierce ones met again.
sentences.n: ‘Næs … long tō ðon’ is ‘it was not long until then’, ‘þæt … gemētton’ ‘that they met’. ‘ðā āglǣcean’ is a plural: the word that has been used of the dragon and of Grendel is now used of both combatants. ‘hȳ’ is ‘they’, and ‘eft’ ‘again’. Man and monster now carry the same name.

sentences.t:
Hyrte hyne hordweard, hreðer ǣðme wēoll,
nīwan stefne;
sentences.l: The hoard-guard took heart, the breast heaved with breath, with a new turn;
sentences.i: The guardian of the hoard took heart again, his breast heaving with breath;
sentences.n: ‘Hyrte hyne’ is ‘heartened himself’ (‘hyrtan’ ‘encourage’ with a reflexive pronoun), and ‘hreðer ǣðme wēoll’ ‘his breast welled with breath’, a dative of means. ‘nīwan stefne’ is ‘with a new turn’, ‘afresh’, a dative (as at 1787): ‘stefn’ here means ‘time, turn’ rather than ‘voice’, as the lexica give it for this phrase.

sentences.t:
nearo ðrōwode
fȳre befongen sē ðe ǣr folce wēold.
sentences.l: he suffered distress, encircled by fire, who once ruled a people.
sentences.i: He who had once ruled a people now suffered hardship, wrapped in fire.
sentences.n: ‘nearo ðrōwode’ is ‘suffered distress’ (‘nearu’ ‘narrowness, hardship’, an accusative of what is suffered), ‘fȳre befongen’ ‘encircled by fire’, and ‘sē ðe ǣr folce wēold’ ‘he who earlier ruled a people’, Beowulf. The poet turns from the dragon back to the man, and names him by his former rank.

sentences.t:
Nealles him on hēape handgesteallan,
æðelinga bearn ymbe gestōdon
hildecystum, ac hȳ on holt bugon,
ealdre burgan.
sentences.l: Not at all around him in a troop did his hand-companions, the sons of athelings, stand with battle-virtues, but they turned to the wood, to save their lives.
sentences.i: His hand-companions, the sons of noblemen, did not stand about him in a band with the courage of warriors; they fled into the wood to save their lives.
sentences.n: ‘Nealles’ is ‘not at all’ and the verb is ‘gestōdon’ with ‘ymbe’, ‘stood about’. ‘handgesteallan’ is ‘hand-companions’ (‘hand’ ‘hand’ + ‘gesteall’ ‘companion’), the retainers. Klaeber’s italic ‘a’ marks an alteration; the apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘heand’, and Kemble’s ‘hand’ is the repair. ‘æðelinga bearn’ is ‘sons of princes’ (the best-born young men) and ‘hildecystum’ ‘with battle-virtues’ (‘cyst’ as at 2543). ‘on holt bugon’ is ‘turned (fled) to the wood’ (‘būgan’, ‘bend, flee’), and ‘ealdre burgan’ ‘to save their lives’ (‘beorgan’ with a dative). These are the men who came with Beowulf to the barrow (2401–2410).

sentences.t:
Hiora in ānum wēoll
sefa wið sorgum;
sentences.l: In one of them the heart welled against sorrows;
sentences.i: In one of them, though, the heart surged with grief;
sentences.n: ‘Hiora’ is ‘of them’, genitive plural, and ‘in ānum’ ‘in one’: one man among the rest. ‘wēoll’ is ‘welled, surged’ (the same verb as of the father’s sorrow at 2464), and ‘sefa wið sorgum’ ‘the heart against sorrows’, where ‘wið’ may mean that his heart struggled with sorrows or surged amid them. The poet does not name him here.

sentences.t:
sibb’ ǣfre ne mæg
wiht onwendan þām ðe wēl þenceð.
sentences.l: kinship nothing can ever turn aside for him who thinks well.
sentences.i: For the man who thinks rightly, nothing can ever turn kinship aside.
sentences.n: ‘sibb’’ is ‘sibbe’ (‘kinship, family bond’) with the final vowel dropped before ‘ǣfre’ (the apostrophe is Klaeber’s). It is the object of ‘onwendan’ (‘turn aside’); ‘wiht’ is ‘thing, at all’, and I take it as the subject, ‘nothing’, with ‘ne mæg’ (‘cannot’) negating it. ‘þām ðe wēl þenceð’ is ‘for him who thinks well’, a dative. This is the poet’s maxim, set between the scene of the retainers’ flight and the arrival of the one who stayed.
